rows.meaning: This first branch asks what a Bitcoin transaction is before any of its bytes are read
rows.analogy: A transaction is a signed letter asking every ledger to update itself.

rows.meaning: This group collects the three ideas a reader needs before the bytes make sense: the transaction itself, the ownership record that it asks full nodes to change, and the parts that every transaction is built from
rows.analogy: a signed letter that asks every ledger to change

rows.meaning: A transaction is the data Alice uses to convince every full node to update its database so that some bitcoins she controls are recorded as controlled by Bob.
rows.analogy: a signed letter asking every bank branch to update its ledger.

rows.concept: The ownership record of a full node
rows.meaning: Every full node keeps its own copy of the database that says which bitcoins are controlled by whom, and a transaction is accepted when the node agrees to update that copy.
rows.analogy: a land register that every town keeps an identical copy of.

rows.meaning: A serialized transaction has a version, an inputs field, an outputs field, a lock time and, when it spends segwit outputs, a marker, a flag and a witness structure.
rows.analogy: a cheque with boxes for payer, payee, amount and signature.

rows.meaning: Serialization is the writing of a data structure as a sequence of bytes so that it can be stored, hashed or sent
rows.analogy: packing a letter flat for the post

rows.meaning: A serialized transaction is the transaction written as the sequence of bytes that Bitcoin Core hashes, relays and stores; the book prints Alice's as 388 hexadecimal characters.
rows.analogy: a letter flattened into one long strip of tape.

rows.meaning: The extended serialization format of BIP144 adds a marker byte, a flag byte and a witness structure to the legacy layout, for transactions that spend segwit outputs.
rows.analogy: the same letter with a signed slip tucked in at the end.

rows.meaning: Legacy serialization is the original transaction format, without the marker, flag and witness structure; it is still used for every transaction that spends no witness program.
rows.analogy: the plain letter, before the extra slip was invented.

rows.meaning: The partially signed bitcoin transaction (PSBT) format of BIPs 174 and 370 lets an untrusted program build a transaction template that trusted programs holding the keys verify and complete.
rows.analogy: a form passed round the office until every signer has signed.

rows.meaning: A byte map draws a serialized transaction with each field at its byte position and length, so that the hexadecimal can be read as named parts.
rows.analogy: a floor plan showing which room each byte lives in.

rows.meaning: This branch reads the first six bytes of Alice's transaction: the four-byte version and, because her transaction carries a witness, the marker and the flag that announce the extended format
rows.analogy: Version, marker and flag are the edition number and labels on the envelope.

rows.meaning: The version field is the four-byte little-endian integer at the start of every transaction
rows.analogy: the edition number printed on a form

rows.meaning: Version 1 is the original transaction version, written 01000000 in little-endian order; every transaction must follow its rules, and Alice's transaction uses it.
rows.analogy: edition 1 of a form, still valid in every office.

rows.meaning: Version 2 transactions were introduced by the BIP68 soft fork; only in a transaction of version 2 or higher is a sequence value below 2 to the 31 a relative timelock, and BIP112's opcode fails below version 2.
rows.analogy: edition 2, which adds a waiting-period box to the form.

rows.meaning: The version 3 proposal, BIP431, changes only the relay policy of full nodes: a version 3 transaction accepts topological restrictions in exchange for protection against pinning attacks; Bitcoin Core treats it as standard since release 28.0.
rows.analogy: a draft edition that offices may choose to accept.

rows.meaning: A presigned transaction is signed but not broadcast, perhaps for years; a later rule that applies to its version could make it permanently invalid, so new constraints are reserved for new version numbers.
rows.analogy: a post-dated cheque kept in a drawer.

rows.meaning: The marker and the flag are the two bytes that follow the version in the extended serialization format
rows.analogy: a fragile label on a parcel

rows.meaning: The marker is the byte 0x00 after the version of an extended-format transaction; a legacy parser would read it as a count of zero inputs, which no transaction can have, so it signals the extended format.
rows.analogy: a sticker on a parcel saying special contents inside.

rows.meaning: The flag is the byte after the marker; it is 0x01 in the current protocol, other values are reserved for upgrades, and BIP144 reads it as a bit vector for adding non-committed data later.
rows.analogy: a second sticker that names the kind of extras.

rows.meaning: This branch reads the inputs field of a transaction, the 42 bytes of Alice's transaction that say where the bitcoins she spends come from
rows.analogy: Inputs are the banknotes you hand over, each named by its address.

rows.meaning: The input list is the inputs field as a whole: a count followed by that many inputs
rows.analogy: a receipt listing the notes you hand over

rows.meaning: The input count is the compactSize integer that opens the inputs field; it must be at least one, and transaction size limits keep it to a few thousand in practice.
rows.analogy: counting how many cheques are stapled to a payment.

rows.meaning: A compactSize unsigned integer is one byte for values up to 252 and otherwise a prefix byte 0xfd, 0xfe or 0xff followed by the value as a 2-, 4- or 8-byte little-endian integer.
rows.analogy: a ticket machine: small numbers get short tickets.

rows.meaning: Bitcoin programs use several variable-length integers: compactSize in transactions and the P2P protocol, Bitcoin Core's VarInts in its UTXO database, and the unrelated Compact encoding of a block header's nBits field.
rows.analogy: three kinds of ticket sold under one name.

rows.meaning: The outpoint is the field with which an input points at the previous output it spends
rows.analogy: a street address with building and flat

rows.meaning: An outpoint is the 32-byte txid of a previous transaction followed by the 4-byte index of one of its outputs; every input has exactly one, and a node uses it to find the output being spent.
rows.analogy: a street address: building number plus flat number.

rows.meaning: The txid in an outpoint is the 32-byte double-SHA-256 identifier of the transaction that created the output being spent, stored in internal byte order.
rows.analogy: the building number in that address.

rows.meaning: The output index is the 4-byte unsigned integer after the txid in an outpoint; it chooses one output of the previous transaction, counting from zero.
rows.analogy: the flat number inside the building, counted from zero.

rows.meaning: One of Bitcoin's consensus rules forbids any output from being spent more than once within a valid blockchain: Alice cannot use the same previous output to pay both Bob and Carol.
rows.analogy: a banknote that can be handed over only once.

rows.meaning: Two transactions that each try to spend the same previous output are conflicting transactions; only one of them can be included in a valid blockchain.
rows.analogy: two cheques written against the same banknote.

rows.meaning: Bitcoin Core keeps a database of every unspent transaction output with essential metadata; each new block removes the outputs its transactions spend and adds the outputs they create.
rows.analogy: a drawer holding only the banknotes nobody has spent.

rows.meaning: This group explains the book's sidebar on the two byte orders of a hash
rows.analogy: a book you can read from the front or the back

rows.meaning: A digest is the output of a hash function; Bitcoin uses digests as identifiers of blocks and transactions, in commitments, and in proof of work.
rows.analogy: a fingerprint taken from a whole document.

rows.meaning: Internal byte order is the order in which a digest's bytes appear within transactions and blocks and are fed to hash functions; the book also calls it little-endian.
rows.analogy: reading a phone number from its last digit.

rows.meaning: Display byte order is the reversed form in which identifiers are shown to users and accepted by explorers and bitcoin-cli; the book also calls it big-endian.
rows.analogy: reading the phone number the usual way round.

rows.meaning: The input script is the second field of every input, after the outpoint and before the sequence, and it is length-prefixed
rows.analogy: a keyhole that legacy inputs fill with the key

rows.meaning: The input script is the legacy field in which a spending transaction places its signatures and other authorising data; a segwit input leaves it empty.
rows.analogy: the key you hand over at the door.

rows.meaning: The length prefix is the compactSize integer before an input script that says how many bytes of script follow; it is 0x6b for the book's 107-byte example and 0x00 for Alice's empty script.
rows.analogy: a label on a box saying how many items it holds.

rows.meaning: This branch reads the last four bytes of an input, which the book calls its sequence number, and follows the three meanings the field has carried
rows.analogy: The sequence field is a booth ticket whose meaning changed three times.

rows.meaning: The original sequence-based replacement is the first meaning of the field: the book says the sequence field was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation, the sequence number tracking the version of the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
rows.analogy: an order slip you can reissue until the kitchen closes

rows.meaning: The sequence is the 4-byte field that ends every input; its maximal value 0xffffffff, called final, opts out of replacement, of the BIP125 signal and of any relative timelock.
rows.analogy: a counter on a ticket that the booth can reissue.

rows.meaning: The setup transaction deposits Alice's and Bob's money into a multisignature output that needs both signatures; the refund transaction, with sequence 0, pays each their deposit back and is kept unbroadcast.
rows.analogy: a locked deposit box that needs two keys.

rows.meaning: A payment channel is a protocol in which two parties sign many versions of one transaction off the chain, each with a higher sequence, and broadcast only the final one; the book's card game is the original form.
rows.analogy: a bar tab: many orders, one bill at the end.

rows.meaning: Unlimited free replacement let an attacker with 1,000 replacements a minute at 200 bytes each cost 50,000 relaying nodes about 10 GB of bandwidth a minute for 20 KB of their own, so the scheme was disabled.
rows.analogy: refiling the same form again and again to clog the office.

rows.meaning: Replace-by-fee is the second meaning of the sequence field
rows.analogy: outbidding someone at an auction

rows.meaning: Opt-in replace-by-fee is the relay policy under which a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate replaces an unconfirmed one that signalled replaceability; the replacement must also pay for its own relay.
rows.analogy: outbidding someone at an auction

rows.meaning: By BIP125 an unconfirmed transaction with any input whose sequence is below 0xfffffffe, at least two below the maximum, signals that it may be replaced by a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate.
rows.analogy: a tick box marked amendable on the form.

rows.meaning: The relative timelock is the third meaning of the sequence field and the only one enforced by consensus
rows.analogy: a gift card that activates a week after purchase

rows.meaning: Under BIP68 a version 2 input with sequence below 2 to the 31 may only be confirmed once the output it spends has aged by the sequence's value: a lock of 30 blocks allows confirmation with at least 29 blocks between the two.
rows.analogy: a coupon valid only some days after purchase.

rows.meaning: The type flag is bit 22 of the sequence, value 1 shifted left 22; set, the lock counts units of 512 seconds, clear, it counts blocks.
rows.analogy: a switch choosing between counting turns and counting minutes.

rows.meaning: The disable flag is bit 31 of the sequence; an input with it set has no relative timelock even in a version 2 transaction, so a transaction may mix locked and unlocked inputs.
rows.analogy: an off switch that makes the coupon valid at once.

rows.meaning: Only the 16 least significant bits of the sequence carry the relative timelock, so the mask 0x0000ffff extracts a value of at most 65,535, which in blocks or in 512-second units is a bit more than a year.
rows.analogy: a counter with room for only 65,535 ticks.

rows.meaning: This branch reads the outputs field, the 75 bytes of Alice's transaction that assign her bitcoins to new conditions
rows.analogy: Outputs are the lines of a till receipt: an amount and who may collect it.

rows.meaning: The output list is the outputs field as a whole: a compactSize count greater than zero, then that many outputs, each an 8-byte amount and a length-prefixed script
rows.analogy: the change a till hands back

rows.meaning: The output count is the compactSize integer that opens the outputs field; it must be greater than zero, and Alice's transaction has two outputs.
rows.analogy: how many envelopes of money leave the till.

rows.meaning: The amount is the first field of an output: an 8-byte signed little-endian integer of satoshis, called value in Bitcoin Core; Alice's first output carries 20,000.
rows.analogy: the sum on a cheque, written in the smallest coins.

rows.meaning: A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin an on-chain transaction can represent; there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin, so 20,000 satoshis are 0.0002 bitcoin.
rows.analogy: a cent that is a hundred-millionth of the whole note.

rows.concept: The consensus range of an amount
rows.meaning: Consensus allows an output amount from zero to 21 million bitcoins, 2.1 quadrillion satoshis; Bitcoin Core names the maximum MAX_MONEY and refuses negative, oversized and overflowing totals.
rows.analogy: a cheque form that cannot print negative or absurd sums.

rows.meaning: This group explains the outputs that are not worth spending and the relay policy against creating them
rows.analogy: a bank that refuses to count single cents

rows.meaning: An uneconomical output is one whose value is less than the extra fee that spending it would add to a transaction; a zero-value output is always uneconomical, and others become so when fee rates rise.
rows.analogy: a coin so small the postage costs more than the coin.

rows.meaning: Bitcoin Core's dust threshold is the size of an output plus the smallest input that could spend it, times the dust relay rate of 3,000 satoshis per kilo-vbyte: 546 satoshis for a legacy P2PKH output, 294 for a P2WPKH output.
rows.analogy: the smallest coin the post office agrees to carry.

rows.meaning: A data-carrier output is one whose script begins with OP_RETURN; it can never be spent, so nodes need not keep it, and Bitcoin Core's dust policy allows it a value of zero.
rows.analogy: a note stuck on a parcel, carrying no money.

rows.meaning: The output script is the last field of an output: the book says the amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins, and that according to consensus the minimum size of an output script is zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
rows.analogy: the lock fitted to a new deposit box

rows.meaning: The output script holds the conditions for spending an output; Alice's first is a 34-byte segwit version 1 script for Bob, her second a 22-byte segwit version 0 script for her change.
rows.analogy: a lock fitted to the coin: whoever opens it may spend.

rows.meaning: Consensus sets the minimum size of an output script at zero and no explicit maximum when it is created, but a later transaction can only spend an output whose script is 10,000 bytes or smaller.
rows.analogy: a cap on how long the lock's instructions may be.

rows.meaning: An anyone-can-spend script is one anyone can satisfy, such as the empty output script spent by an input script of OP_TRUE; upgrades take such a script and add constraints to it.
rows.analogy: a safe left unlocked in the street.

rows.meaning: Standard transaction outputs are the few output script templates that Bitcoin Core's policy for relaying and mining transactions allows, kept to support upgrades and to encourage putting conditions in redeem, witness and leaf scripts.
rows.analogy: the few lock models the post office accepts.

rows.meaning: This branch explains the witness structure, the 67 bytes near the end of Alice's transaction that prove she was allowed to spend
rows.analogy: A witness is the ID you show at the counter, kept off the receipt.

rows.meaning: This group explains what a witness is before any byte of it is read
rows.analogy: the ID card you show at the counter

rows.meaning: A witness is data that solves the math problem protecting an output, which full nodes check instead of trusting; for the script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL the witness is the value 2.
rows.analogy: the answer to the riddle printed on the lock.

rows.concept: Public key and signature as witness
rows.meaning: In a digital signature scheme the public key is a public identifier of secret data and the signature a solution to an equation only the holder of that data can produce; a script of a public key and OP_CHECKSIG makes the signature the witness.
rows.analogy: a signature only the account holder can produce.

rows.meaning: A contract protocol is a series of transactions between parties, often signed out of order so that each party is protected before committing; the payment channel is one, and such protocols exposed the problems with witnesses in the input script.
rows.analogy: agreements signed in advance so nobody can walk away.

rows.meaning: This group states the three problems that the book found with placing witnesses in the input script: the circular dependency, in which a refund cannot be signed before the deposit whose identifier it needs; third-party transaction malleability, in which anyone can re-encode a push in an input script and change a transaction's identifier; and second-party malleability, in which a counterparty can produce an alternative signature and change it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
rows.analogy: re-spelling a name so the filing clerk loses the receipt

rows.meaning: A circular dependency arises when Alice and Bob want to sign a refund before the deposit it spends, but in the legacy format the deposit's txid depends on its signatures, so the refund cannot be built until both have signed the deposit.
rows.analogy: needing the key to get the key.

rows.meaning: Unwanted third-party transaction malleability is a stranger's ability to change a transaction's txid without invalidating it, for example by re-encoding a push in the input script, so that a conflicting copy confirms and any transaction spending the original's outputs becomes invalid.
rows.analogy: a stranger rewording your cheque without changing the sum.

rows.meaning: The number 2 can be pushed as OP_2, as a one-byte push, as a two-byte push or with OP_PUSHDATA1; each is a different byte string, so each gives a legacy transaction a different txid while the script result is the same.
rows.analogy: four ways to write the same number in words.

rows.meaning: Unwanted second-party transaction malleability is a counterparty's ability to produce an alternative signature, because a signer chooses a random number each time, and so a conflicting transaction with a different txid that invalidates a presigned refund.
rows.analogy: your partner re-signing a document with another pen.

rows.meaning: Some malleability is wanted: with a signature hash the sender can allow others to change parts of a transaction, as when Bob adds an input to help pay Alice's fee; the book says unwanted when it means the other kind.
rows.analogy: a form with a box for changes allowed by me.

rows.meaning: Segregated witness, segwit, is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid
rows.analogy: keeping the passport photo off the ticket number

rows.meaning: Segregated witness is the separation of a transaction's witness from the data its txid is computed over; an empty input script keeps witnesses from affecting the txid and so removes circular dependencies and both unwanted malleabilities.
rows.analogy: keeping the passport photo off the ticket number

rows.meaning: A hard fork is a change to the consensus rules that is not compatible with older full nodes; the obvious way to implement segwit needed one, which is why an alternative was sought.
rows.analogy: a new road standard that old cars cannot drive on.

rows.meaning: A soft fork is a backward-compatible change to the consensus rules: full nodes with the change must not accept any block that nodes without it would consider invalid, so new nodes can reject blocks old nodes accept but not the reverse.
rows.analogy: a stricter road rule that old cars can still obey.

rows.meaning: A witness program is the data in a segwit output script: a script of a number from 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes is the segwit template, the number its version and the data the witness program; old nodes may spend it with an empty input script, new nodes require one.
rows.analogy: a lock label saying which kind of key fits.

rows.meaning: The witness structure is the field added by segwit to hold the data that an input script may no longer carry; it sits after the outputs and before the lock time and is not part of the txid.
rows.analogy: an annex page stapled to the transaction.

rows.meaning: This group reads the bytes of the witness structure
rows.analogy: annex pages bound behind the main letter

rows.meaning: A witness stack is the part of the witness structure belonging to one input: a compactSize count of items followed by the items; there is one stack per input, so the structure has no count of its own.
rows.analogy: a pile of papers handed in for one input.

rows.meaning: A witness item is one element of a witness stack, prefixed by a compactSize integer giving its size; Alice's single item is a 65-byte signature.
rows.analogy: one sheet in the pile, with its length stamped on.

rows.meaning: A legacy input in a segwit transaction has a witness stack consisting entirely of a count of zero, 0x00, so the structure stays one stack per input.
rows.analogy: an empty annex: nothing stapled to old-style inputs.

rows.meaning: This branch covers the last field of every transaction and the first transaction of every block
rows.analogy: A lock time is a post-dated cheque; a coinbase is the mint's wage slip.

rows.meaning: The lock time is the four-byte field that ends every transaction
rows.analogy: a post-dated cheque

rows.meaning: The lock time is the last 4 bytes of a transaction; zero makes it eligible for any block, and since block 31,000 a non-zero value is a consensus rule restricting which blocks may include it.
rows.analogy: a do-not-open-before date on an envelope.

rows.concept: Lock time as a block height
rows.meaning: A lock time below 500,000,000 is a block height: the transaction can only be included in a block whose height is equal to the lock time or higher, so 123,456 allows block 123,456 and any later one.
rows.analogy: do not open before a numbered page of the logbook.

rows.concept: Lock time as an epoch time
rows.meaning: A lock time of 500,000,000 or more is an epoch time, seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00 UTC; the transaction can only be included in a block whose median time past is greater than the lock time.
rows.analogy: do not open before this calendar date.

rows.meaning: The median time past (MTP) of a block is the median of the timestamps of the last eleven blocks; time locks are compared with it, and it is normally an hour or two behind the clock.
rows.analogy: asking the middle voter, not the loudest.

rows.meaning: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block
rows.analogy: the mint's wage slip for the miner

rows.meaning: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction of a block, created by its miner to claim the block's fees and, until the subsidy runs out, newly created bitcoins; older documents call it a generation transaction.
rows.analogy: the bonus the mint pays whoever closes the page.

rows.meaning: A coinbase transaction's single input must have an outpoint with a null txid of all zeros and the maximal output index 0xffffffff, so that it cannot reference a previous output.
rows.analogy: a ticket with no previous holder: printed new.

rows.meaning: The coinbase field is the coinbase transaction's input-script field, 2 to 100 bytes long, not executed, and since BIP34 beginning with a push of the block height; it gives the transaction its name.
rows.analogy: a free text box on the bonus slip.

rows.meaning: The block subsidy is the newly created bitcoin a coinbase may claim: 50 BTC at first, halved every 210,000 blocks and rounded down to the satoshi, so that the total issued is just under 21 million.
rows.analogy: a bonus that halves every four years of work.

rows.meaning: The block reward is the total a miner can claim for a block, the fees of its transactions plus the subsidy; the coinbase's outputs may sum to no more than it.
rows.analogy: the bonus plus the tips from customers.

rows.meaning: The maturity rule says a transaction spending a coinbase output cannot be included in any block until the coinbase has 100 confirmations; outputs with fewer are called immature.
rows.analogy: wages you cannot spend until the pay clears.

rows.meaning: This last branch has two jobs
rows.analogy: Weight is a transaction's postage; foundations are the post office's rules.

rows.meaning: Weight is the modern unit in which the size of a transaction or a block is measured, and vbytes are weight divided by four
rows.analogy: postage that charges less for the small print

rows.meaning: Weight is BIP141's measure of a transaction: the legacy serialization's size times 3 plus the full serialization's size, which is 569 for Alice's transaction, the figure Bitcoin Core reports.
rows.analogy: postage priced by volume, with signatures at a discount.

rows.meaning: A vbyte is a quarter of a weight unit, rounded up, so that a legacy transaction's vbytes equal its bytes; Alice's transaction is 143 vbytes.
rows.analogy: the parcel size after the discount is applied.

rows.meaning: Blocks are limited to 4,000,000 weight, Bitcoin Core's MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT; the header and the transaction count take a small fixed share and the rest is for transactions.
rows.analogy: a lorry that carries four million weight units.

rows.meaning: Each field's weight is its serialized size times a factor: 4 for the version, inputs, outputs and lock time, 1 for the marker, the flag and the witness structure; summed over Alice's transaction the factors give 569.
rows.analogy: a price list: four for plain bytes, one for annex bytes.

rows.meaning: This group explains the terms the chapter uses on every page without a section of its own
rows.analogy: the foundations under a house

rows.meaning: A hash function maps input of any length to a fixed-length digest, one-way and unpredictable, so that a digest can identify data and commit to it; Bitcoin's is SHA-256, with a 32-byte output.
rows.analogy: a meat grinder: any input, a result of fixed size.

rows.meaning: Bitcoin's identifiers are double SHA-256: the hash function applied to its own output, so a txid is SHA-256 of SHA-256 of the legacy serialization, shown reversed.
rows.analogy: running the grinder twice for safety.

rows.meaning: The txid is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's legacy serialization, displayed in reversed byte order; for a segwit transaction it therefore excludes the witness.
rows.analogy: a parcel's tracking number from its plain contents.

rows.meaning: The wtxid is the double SHA-256 of the whole extended serialization, witness included; it changes when the witness changes, and blocks commit to it separately from the txid.
rows.analogy: a tracking number that counts the annex too.

rows.meaning: Relay policy is the set of rules a full node applies to unconfirmed transactions it relays and keeps in its memory pool; it is chosen by the node, can change, and includes dust, standardness, version 3 and replacement rules.
rows.analogy: the house rules of one post office.

rows.meaning: A consensus rule is a rule every full node enforces identically to decide which blocks and transactions are valid; this chapter's examples are the input and output bounds, the amount range, BIP68, the lock time, the subsidy and the maturity rule.
rows.analogy: the law every post office must obey identically.
